extracted.intended_audience: readers of entertainment/feminist cultural criticism and general online audience interested in comedy and #MeToo discourse
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance implicit in an opinion piece about a comedian's remarks and press tour, focusing on what makes public commentary or comedy responsible or irresponsible regarding sexual misconduct, racism, and critique of other works. Includes expectations for accuracy, empathy, and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not blame victims for speaking out / avoid victim-blaming
rubrics_metrics.description: Macdonald is operating from that victim-blaming perspective of somehow believing that because so many more women and other survivors are now talking about their experiences with abuse, they must be the cause of that increase in abuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that increased reporting reflects survivors speaking up, not an increase in abuse caused by the movement. Avoid framing survivors as the problem for bringing abuse to light; understand power dynamics that make speaking out risky.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give survivors the benefit of the doubt; don't overstate false allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘statistically, false accusations are extremely rare so maybe let’s give women the benefit of the doubt before we assume they’re lying.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rhetoric that implies large-scale dishonesty by victims. When discussing allegations, acknowledge the rarity of false accusations and the costs to people who come forward; don't use hypothetical or exceptional cases to undermine broad claims of abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute consequences to perpetrators' actions rather than to the #MeToo movement
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of phrasing like C.K.’s career being 'derailed by #MeToo' rather than by his own actions, exemplified by the line: 'YOUR CAREER WAS NOT “DERAILED” BY #MeToo IT WAS DERAILED BECAUSE YOU DECIDED THAT WOMEN NEEDED TO SEE YOU JERK OFF WHETHER THEY WANTED TO OR NOT (THEY DID NOT)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing fallout, name the conduct that caused it (e.g., sexual harassment, assault) instead of blaming a movement that exposed that conduct. Avoid language that frames accountability as an external attack rather than a consequence of harmful behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be informed and observant before making claims about social problems
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘He also admits in the interview that he didn’t really believe racism was a problem (because Obama) until he watched Sacha Baron Cohen’s new show. ... Hard to make observational humor when you’re not like… observing.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public figures and comedians should base commentary on facts and lived realities; educate yourself about systemic issues before dismissing them. Observational humor requires genuine observation and awareness, not willful ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not criticize works you haven't seen
rubrics_metrics.description: Norm Macdonald also said he hasn’t seen Hannah Gadsby’s brilliant stand-up special Nanette, and then proceeds to talk about why it’s not actually comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid publicly critiquing creative works you haven't experienced. If you comment without having seen the work, disclose that and refrain from definitive judgments; doing otherwise undermines credibility and is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid normalizing or privately facilitating accused abusers without addressing harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Macdonald says that he recently reached out to both Louis C.K. and Roseanne Barr and put them in touch with one another. Following her firing from ABC, Barr was 'just so broken and just crying constantly.' So she and C.K. had a 'good conversation' and Macdonald said they 'were just giving any advice you could give to each other.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing emotional support or helping accused figures reconnect can be perceived as normalizing or minimizing their wrongdoing if done without acknowledging victims' experiences. Public figures should be cautious about facilitating or humanizing accused individuals without accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not minimize victims' suffering by comparing it to perpetrators' career loss
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘There are very few people that have gone through what they have, losing everything in a day,’ he said. 'Of course, people will go, 'What about the victims?' But you know what? The victims didn’t have to go through that.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid framing the loss of a perpetrator’s career as equivalent to the harm experienced by victims. Accountability consequences are not comparable to the trauma and long-term effects of abuse; comparisons that minimize victims are inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use responsible phrasing in reporting and profiles (avoid blaming movements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of profiles describing C.K.’s career as 'derailed by #MeToo' rather than 'derailed by his own actions,' and the author noting 'Really sick of this kind of phrasing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists and writers should choose language that accurately reflects causation and responsibility. Avoid understating perpetrators' culpability by implying that social movements are the primary agents of consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful that press tours amplify statements; avoid harmful publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Anyway, good luck with your show Norm Macdonald. Your press tour sure is off to a hell of a start.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that press appearances spread views widely; avoid using promotional platforms to make statements that dismiss or harm survivors or that reveal ignorance. Publicity should not be used to normalize problematic viewpoints.
